chapter: Navy years and attitudes toward whites
title: Family and whites; touring the South in the civil rights era
summary: His family had no trouble with whites; on tour he was treated well, with stories of Mississippi and a dance hall where bands played each song twice.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Something we haven't really talked about, and we can get back to that, to what you did. What did your parents tell you about whites, about whites, and how to behave?

You know, okay, first of all, I can say this. You see, my family being the type of people that they were, we never did have no white problem. We never had no white. You know what, I think it's because I think being from a decent family, I think we were kind of looked on as just poor, decent people. Now there always was that other kind, that other person, you know, them other people. But my family, we never had no problem. And I say that, to say this, even during the civil rights struggle with me, playing music, I remember going from New Orleans through Mississippi, to what, that's Ole Miss or Mississippi State, which one of them is all the way up there to Memphis? Playing there. Leaving here going all the way through, and it was doing the height of the struggle. Do you know what they were there? No problem. And I remember one man, one white fellow we met coming back, he said, you fellas, well we stopped and put in the station to get games. He said, y'all must be pretty tired and hungry. We said, we are. Here's a restaurant. He said, look, y'all go in there? He said, no, no, count the long time. He said, order whatever you want. He said, nobody's going to tell you nothing, because this is my place. But what I'm saying is this, I think it's individual. It's always individual things. Now, I know I have went behind bands, and I ain't going to call their names, I can call their names of some bands that was terrible out there. I went behind bands, played the same place they played, had no trouble. The band preceded me out before me, and I was all the trouble in the world. But I think it was always the individual. First of all, see, when I say band, I'm talking about my original untouchable. That was me, Justin Adams, Dalton Russo, David Francois, and you know, all decent people. And we just never had no problem. It's them other people that went before us, they brought their problems with them. But here I come, and always were treated nice. But I tell you one incident. We were playing at Mississippi Southern, playing a ball. And I forget, all the white people dressed, they were dressing black and white. And Frank Pena had booked us, and so they'll ask. I had to go call, no, Frank called for me. So they came and got me on stage to go answer the phone. Now you know what the guy told me? He said, tell me, he said, look, he said, just try not to bump into nobody, because I had to go through that crowd of people. I made it through. But you see, like I said, now, I could have been this boisterous, like I said, I could have went through the people and made trouble for myself. But I didn't. Now, playing right up here in, in, up Highway 90, what is that? Right past Lutcher, the first town up there where the sugar mill is. No, no, going to, going towards Lulon. What is that? Highway, Highway 90. Yeah. Throwing up to, they had this little club there, but I know Sugar Barton played there, he probably, if you interview him, he going to tell you. But anyway, in this club, well, we had to play every song twice. It was a white dance hall for youngsters. Every song you play, you play it twice. You never heard that before. You never played, you had to, that was the trend of the town. I'm going to think of the name of it in a minute. Every song you play, you play it twice. You play it once and they stay in there. And you play it again. But now, what I, what I think to say is that we didn't, we didn't have, they, they bring us whatever, everything we wanted, but was brought on a bandstand. And we had to go to the bathroom, you walk off the bandstand, you walk side the bandstand, on down there, to the bathroom, come back. And then you come back, walk down, but you stayed on the bandstand. What's the name of this? Oh boy, I can't think of it. You know.
